strengths: Broad empirical evaluation spanning both unimodal (mathematical reasoning) and four multimodal task categories (visual reasoning, geometry reasoning, classification, reasoning grounding), across multiple base models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Qwen2-VL-2B, Qwen2.5-VL-3B).
Clear practical motivation: reducing memory/compute by removing critic and reference models is valuable for the community, and the method is simple to implement (Algorithm 1 is a few lines).
Reasonably thorough set of ablations (group size, reward normalization strategy, effect of re-adding KL constraint) that support some of the design choices.
The comparison table (Table 11) juxtaposing loss/advantage formulations of PPO/GRPO/Dr.GRPO/DAPO/GPG is a useful summary for readers unfamiliar with the design space.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: GPG is essentially the group-normalized REINFORCE estimator already implicit in GRPO once the PPO-style clipping term is removed (which is inactive when ratio=1, i.e., a single gradient step per rollout, as is common practice). The paper's central claim of "directly optimizing the original RL objective instead of a surrogate" is not rigorously established — in the single-update, on-policy regime the GRPO surrogate gradient coincides with the plain policy-gradient estimator, so the distinction claimed in the introduction is overstated. Several existing works already remove KL (DAPO), remove the critic (ReMax, REINFORCE++, Dr.GRPO) or study reward normalization (Dr. GRPO); GPG largely recombines these known simplifications rather than introducing a new mechanism.

No importance-sampling ratio or old-policy reuse is included, and the paper does not discuss what happens when multiple gradient updates are taken per rollout batch (a common practical setting); the theoretical justification for omitting the ratio term entirely (rather than only in the single-update, on-policy limit) is missing or hand-waved.

The advantage formula (Eq. 6, group mean/std normalization) is essentially identical to GRPO's advantage — the paper's own Table 11 confirms A is the same as GRPO's; the actual algorithmic delta versus GRPO is therefore only "drop clip term, drop KL term," which is a fairly small and already partially explored modification.

Several benchmarks (AIME24 with likely only ~30 problems, LISA grounding trained on 239 images, few-shot classification) are very small, so reported gains (e.g., +10 points on AMC23, +10+ points on LISA metrics) could plausibly reflect high-variance single-run noise rather than a robust algorithmic improvement; no variance/multiple-seed results, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported anywhere in the paper.

Missing important baselines given the related work discussed: REINFORCE++ and ReMax are extensively discussed in the introduction as directly relevant simplification approaches but are never empirically compared against GPG; only Dr. GRPO is compared, and only on one table.

The writing is often vague and repetitive with generic claims ("these results underscore the robustness and efficacy," "represents an innovative step forward," "breakthrough") that are not well substantiated by rigorous analysis; the paper reads as engineering-report style rather than providing deep methodological insight into why removing these components helps.

No discussion of training stability/robustness across seeds, nor of failure cases where removing KL/critic could hurt (e.g., larger-scale or longer training runs where policy collapse or reward hacking is more likely without any regularization) — this is a notable gap for a method to be positioned as a general "baseline."

Table 9 shows performance still increasing at group size 16 without an evaluation at larger sizes or discussion of compute-performance tradeoff limits, and the choice of 8 is only weakly justified as a compute/performance tradeoff without a rigorous cost analysis.

strengths: The paper is easy to follow and clearly organized, with a useful comparative table (Table 11) laying out loss functions and advantage functions of competing RL methods (PPO, GRPO, Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GPG) side by side.

A reasonably broad set of empirical settings is covered, spanning unimodal math reasoning (multiple model sizes/benchmarks) and several multimodal tasks (visual reasoning, geometry reasoning, classification, grounding), which gives some breadth to the empirical claims.
Ablations on group size and reward normalization strategy (group vs. batch) are provided and are informative for practitioners.
The method itself is simple to implement (Algorithm 1), and if the reported gains hold up, a simpler and cheaper alternative to GRPO/PPO would be practically useful.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the proposed GPG objective (Eq. 5-6) is essentially vanilla REINFORCE/policy gradient with group-mean-and-std reward normalization used as the advantage, i.e., GRPO stripped of its importance-ratio clipping and KL term. Since training appears to use single on-policy gradient steps per batch, the importance ratio in GRPO is trivially 1, making GPG very close to a straightforward ablation of GRPO rather than a fundamentally new algorithm. The framing as a 'breakthrough' and 'innovative step forward' considerably overstates the technical contribution.

The central claim of 'directly optimizing the original RL objective' instead of a 'surrogate loss' is not rigorously substantiated; no theoretical analysis (bias/variance, convergence) is given to show that removing clipping, KL constraint, and reference/critic models is principled rather than simply an empirically convenient simplification that happens to work in the tested settings.

Important baselines discussed at length in the related work (ReMax, REINFORCE++, RLOO-style methods, DAPO) are never empirically compared against, despite being directly relevant simplifications of PPO/GRPO; only GRPO and (in one table) Dr. GRPO are compared, weakening the claim that GPG is a 'strong baseline' relative to the broader landscape of simplified RL methods.

The comparison methodology is questionable: the paper explicitly states it uses GRPO's hyperparameters for GPG despite acknowledging they are 'suboptimal' for GPG, yet separately tunes/ablates group size and reward normalization for GPG itself (Tables 9-10), raising concerns about whether GRPO was given a comparably fair tuning budget.

Results are mixed rather than uniformly superior: in Table 3, GPG underperforms Dr. GRPO notably on AIME24 (23.3 vs 26.7) and GRPO on AMC23 (60.0 vs 62.5) and MATH-500 (73.6 vs 74.6), which somewhat undercuts the paper's repeated claims of consistent, clear superiority over baselines.

The KL-constraint ablation (Table 10) tests only a single β value (0.04) and draws a strong general conclusion ('constraints negatively impact performance') from this single setting, which is insufficient evidence given KL coefficient is known to be sensitive and task-dependent.

No evaluation on larger-scale models (only up to 7B) is conducted, which the paper itself flags as a limitation, making claims about 'scalability' advantages of removing critic/reference models largely speculative rather than demonstrated.

Reproducibility is undermined by the blank/missing code link in the abstract ('Our code is available at ___'), and several implementation specifics (e.g., exact number of PPO-style epochs per batch, whether importance sampling ratio is used at all) are not fully clarified in the main text.
The qualitative case study (Fig. 2) is a single cherry-picked example and does not constitute rigorous evidence of 'more comprehensive and accurate reasoning capability' as claimed.

Writing in places is overly promotional ('This breakthrough', 'innovative step forward', 'significant advantages for potential scalability') without commensurate rigor, which is a style concern for a technical contribution of this scope.

strengths: The paper provides a clear, well-organized comparison table (Table 1, 11) contrasting GPG with PPO, GRPO, TRPO, DAPO, and Dr.GRPO in terms of which components (value model, reference model, surrogate loss, policy constraint) are used, making the conceptual contribution easy to grasp.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning both unimodal (mathematical reasoning across five benchmarks, two model sizes) and multimodal tasks (visual reasoning, geometry reasoning, classification, reasoning grounding), using multiple established codebases (Open-r1, Open-rs, VisualThinker-R1-Zero, R1-V, Visual-RFT), lending some breadth to the evaluation.
Consistent improvements over GRPO are reported across nearly all tested benchmarks and tasks, which is a positive empirical signal for the proposed simplification.
Useful ablation studies on group size and reward normalization (batch vs. group) and on the effect of adding back a KL constraint, which help clarify some design choices.
The method is simple to implement (Algorithm 1) and the removal of critic/reference models and KL constraint plausibly reduces computational and memory overhead, which is practically appealing.
Code and implementation details are stated to be open-sourced, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: GPG is essentially vanilla REINFORCE with a GRPO-style group-normalized baseline/advantage; it is very closely related to existing REINFORCE-style baselines such as RLOO, ReMax, and REINFORCE++ that are discussed in related work but never empirically compared against in the main experiments, despite being the most directly relevant competitors (all remove the critic and some remove KL/clipping). This omission weakens the empirical case that GPG is meaningfully better than the closest alternatives.

The loss formulation in Eq. 5/Algorithm 1/Table 11 has no importance-sampling ratio term (πθ/πθold), which is only valid under a single gradient update per rollout batch (i.e., on-policy REINFORCE). The paper does not clarify whether multiple gradient steps are taken per batch; if so, the lack of any correction term could introduce a systematic bias/off-policy mismatch that is not discussed or analyzed.

The claim that GPG "directly optimizes the original RL objective" is somewhat overstated: the group-mean/std normalized advantage is itself a biased/heuristic proxy for the true advantage function (not derived from an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator), and no theoretical analysis (bias, variance, or convergence properties) is provided to support the superiority of this specific normalization choice.

The paper cites Dr. GRPO's critique of standard-deviation normalization (which the concurrent work argues introduces bias) but does not address or ablate this critique in the context of GPG, despite using std normalization in its own advantage formula (Eq. 6).

No statistical robustness reporting: RL fine-tuning results are known to have significant run-to-run variance, yet no multiple-seed runs, confidence intervals, or variance estimates are reported for any of the main results tables, making it hard to assess whether reported gains (e.g., 1-3 points on several benchmarks) are statistically meaningful versus noise.

Ablation on group size (Table 9) shows performance still increasing monotonically up to the largest tested group size (16), suggesting the method may not have reached a plateau and raising questions about whether GPG's reported efficiency advantage over GRPO holds when GRPO is also tuned with larger group sizes or other hyperparameters (the paper explicitly states it used GRPO's hyperparameters "despite their suboptimality" for GPG, an asymmetric comparison setup).

Removing the KL constraint entirely could risk reward hacking or degenerate policy drift in more open-ended settings; the paper only tests math/visual tasks with well-specified correctness or IoU rewards, so the generality of a fully constraint-free approach to less verifiable domains is unclear and unaddressed.

Some passages in Sections 3.2 and 5 use promotional, hand-wavy language (e.g., "breakthrough," "innovative step forward," "fosters more open exploration") without corresponding rigorous justification, which detracts from technical precision expected at a top-tier venue.

Evaluation is limited to models up to 7B parameters, and the paper itself acknowledges (Broader Impact) that scalability to much larger models remains untested, limiting confidence in the claimed benefits for state-of-the-art large-scale RFT pipelines.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning unimodal math reasoning (1.5B and 7B models) and four multimodal task categories (visual reasoning, geometry, classification, grounding), with GPG consistently outperforming GRPO baselines across nearly all benchmarks.

The method is conceptually simple and practically appealing: it removes the critic model, reference model, KL constraint, and surrogate clipped loss, which reduces memory and computational cost (e.g., lower GPU memory and training cost than DAPO in Table 9).
Reasonably thorough ablation studies (group size, threshold βth, reward normalization choices, comparison with Dr. GRPO/DAPO) help isolate the contribution of individual design choices.

Additional robustness checks are included, such as evaluation on general-purpose benchmarks (MMLU, C-Eval) to show no degradation in general capability, and pass@k with multiple seeds/standard deviations for the 7B model.

The identification of gradient bias from all-correct/all-incorrect groups (zero-gradient samples) is a reasonable and interpretable observation, and the proposed rescaling (AGE) is simple to implement (Algorithm 1) and integrates well with distributed training without extra communication overhead.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is relatively thin: the method largely amounts to (i) stripping known components from GRPO/PPO (critic, reference model, KL, clipping) and (ii) rescaling the loss by a simple batch-composition factor (B/(B-M)), which is a fairly mechanical normalization rather than a deep methodological advance, yet it is framed as a significant contribution ("breakthrough").

The theoretical justification for removing the reference model and KL constraint is thin; the paper does not discuss potential risks (e.g., reward hacking, policy collapse, distributional drift) over longer training horizons beyond the reported ~1100 steps, nor provide stability guarantees analogous to TRPO/PPO's monotonic improvement arguments.

Fairness of comparisons is questionable: many baseline numbers in Tables 3-4 are taken directly from other papers under different reported settings (marked with symbols) rather than uniformly reproduced, and the authors state they "closely adhere to the hyperparameters employed by GRPO," which are acknowledged to be suboptimal for GRPO itself, potentially biasing comparisons in GPG's favor.

Some reported improvements are surprisingly large for a mostly "subtractive" simplification (e.g., LISA grounding mIoU jump from 34.4 to 51.8, CV-Bench jump of ~17 points), raising concern about whether gains stem from the proposed mechanism versus other confounds (e.g., different effective learning dynamics from removing KL/clipping, hyperparameter differences, or limited-seed variance for these multimodal results, which are not accompanied by error bars).

The derivation of the "accurate gradient estimation" (AGE) correction is more of an algebraic identity than a rigorous debiasing proof; it does not address whether the correction introduces its own biases (e.g., correlation between the number of valid samples in a batch and reward informativeness/gradient magnitude across training).

The paper overclaims significance in several places (e.g., "This breakthrough provides...", "SOTA results"), which is not fully warranted given the relatively narrow scale of experiments (max 7B models) and the incremental nature of the core algorithmic change.

Presentation issues: inconsistent naming (GRPO is sometimes typo'd as "GPRO" in Table 1/15), dense notation, and some claims (e.g., about Dr. GRPO's performance) are stated without careful quantitative context, slightly hurting clarity and rigor of the writing.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple unimodal (AIME24, MATH-500, AMC23, Minerva, OlympiadBench) and multimodal (visual reasoning, geometry, classification, grounding) benchmarks, with consistent improvements over GRPO baselines.

The paper performs a reasonably thorough set of ablations (Fnorm choice, group size, threshold βth, reward normalization, multiple RL method comparisons) that help illuminate which components drive performance.

The overall goal of simplifying RL training for LLM reasoning (removing critic, reference model, KL constraint) is a practically relevant direction, and reduced training cost/memory numbers (e.g., vs DAPO) are reported.
Additional sanity checks on general benchmarks (MMLU, C-Eval, code generation, QA) to show the method does not degrade general capability are a nice addition.
weaknesses: The central technical contribution (the 'Accurate Gradient Estimation' correction α = B/(B-M)) is essentially a trivial renormalization that excludes zero-gradient (all-correct/all-incorrect) samples from the batch average — equivalent to standard masked-mean practice used in many implementations. This is presented as a major novel insight ('reveal the limitations of simplistic debiasing methods', 'accurate gradient estimation technique') but is mathematically unremarkable, and the appendix A 'proof' that PyTorch's distributed averaging is 'incorrect' is essentially restating a well-known masking issue, not a new discovery.

No comparison to RLOO (REINFORCE with Leave-One-Out baseline), which is conceptually very close to the proposed group-mean-baseline policy gradient and is a standard, well-known simplification in this space. This is a significant omission given the paper's claims of being 'the simplest' RL baseline.

The narrative around reward bias is internally inconsistent: without AGE, Fnorm=std (which the paper says introduces 'bias') outperforms Fnorm=1 (45.3 vs 43.9), contradicting the stated goal of avoiding bias; only after adding the α correction does Fnorm=1 pull ahead, and even then Fnorms=std+AGE underperforms Fnorm=1+AGE. This interaction is not theoretically explained, undermining the principled framing of the method and suggesting results are driven by empirical tuning rather than the claimed conceptual insight.

The thresholding/resampling mechanism (βth) introduces additional complexity and a new hyperparameter, which is in tension with the paper's simplicity claims and headline comparison table (Table 2) that shows GPG has 'no' extra components.

Baseline reproduction numbers are inconsistent/favorable to the authors in places (e.g., Oat-Zero-7B reported as 51.4% but reproduced by the authors at 47.8%, a large gap that is not explained), raising concerns about the fairness of some comparisons and casting doubt on the magnitude of claimed improvements.

Main results tables (Table 3, 4, 5-9) report single-run numbers without variance/significance, while the one multi-seed evaluation provided (Table 16, appendix) shows overlapping/noisy standard deviations for several benchmarks (e.g., AIME24, Minerva), suggesting some of the headline margins may not be statistically robust.

The writing contains notable sloppiness (repeated 'GPRO' typo for GRPO in Table 1, inconsistent formatting, vague hardware description 'NPUs from China'), and strong claims (e.g., 'breakthrough', 'SOTA results') are not sufficiently tempered given the largely incremental and empirically-driven nature of the contribution.

Positioning relative to concurrent work Dr. GRPO is somewhat dismissive ('its performance did not significantly outperform GRPO') without deeper analysis of why GPG's similar debiasing idea succeeds where Dr. GRPO's allegedly does not, despite both targeting the same reward/gradient bias issue.

strengths: The paper presents a clean derivation from the classical policy gradient theorem and clearly documents which components of PPO/GRPO/TRPO are removed (value model, reference model, KL constraint, surrogate/clipped loss), summarized helpfully in Table 2 and Table 14.

Very extensive empirical evaluation spanning unimodal math reasoning (1.5B and 7B models, five benchmarks) and four multimodal task families (visual reasoning, geometry reasoning, classification, reasoning grounding), with consistent improvements over GRPO in essentially every setting.

Useful ablations: group size sensitivity, reward normalization choice, threshold β_th, and a systematic component-by-component progression from GRPO to GPG (Table 15) that helps isolate the source of gains.
Comparison against DAPO under matched training steps/dataset shows GPG achieves better or comparable accuracy with lower training cost and memory, which is a meaningful efficiency argument.

Appendix checks for catastrophic forgetting/general-capability regression (MMLU, C-Eval, MBPP, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA) and multi-seed pass@k robustness (Table 16) strengthen the empirical claims beyond single-run comparisons.
The gradient-averaging correction (Appendix A) and its equivalent single-GPU-cost reformulation is a practically relevant contribution for real distributed RL training pipelines.
Detailed reproducibility statement, use of multiple public codebases, and (claimed) anonymous code release.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited: after removing the KL term and critic (already done by prior work such as GRPO/Dr. GRPO/DAPO), the main remaining contribution (the AGE correction, i.e., scaling the loss by B/(B-M)) is mathematically equivalent to simply averaging the loss over valid (non-zero-gradient) samples only, a fairly standard masking/normalization practice; the framing as a novel 'gradient estimation bias' finding somewhat overstates its originality.

Because much of GPG's improvement over the vanilla 'Fnorm=1, α=1' variant comes from this denominator/averaging fix (43.9%→47.8% in Table 1), it raises a fairness question about whether the GRPO/Dr.GRPO baselines being compared against were similarly affected by (or immune to) this same averaging detail in their released implementations — the paper does not clarify this, leaving open the possibility that part of the reported gap is an implementation-detail artifact rather than an algorithmic improvement.

The theoretical argument that Aˆ should not introduce 'reward bias' is stated somewhat informally without rigorous proof of unbiasedness/optimality versus GRPO's std-normalization, and the empirical justification (Table 1) shows the un-normalized variant is not clearly better than GRPO's normalized one, muddying the central claim.

Baseline reproduction numbers vary notably from originally reported values (e.g., Oat-Zero-7B reproduced 47.8 vs. reported 51.4), which could affect the fairness/interpretation of the head-to-head comparisons in Table 4.

Despite billing itself as a 'simple' baseline, the final method still includes several added components (AGE scaling, thresholding β_th, resampling), which somewhat dilutes the simplicity narrative relative to just removing KL/critic/reference model.

No evaluation at larger model scales (e.g., 30B–70B+) to demonstrate the claimed 'scalability' benefits of removing extra components; this is acknowledged as a limitation but weakens the paper's broader claims.

Multimodal experiments use different codebases and training configurations for each task, making it harder to attribute observed gains purely to the algorithmic change versus differences in per-task setup/tuning.
